An idea can have several related representations. Changes of form, scale, order, perspective, or composition can reveal different dependencies and consequences. Similar patterns need not have the same mechanism. A relation useful in one setting may fail in another.

Exploration can branch, combine, reverse, simplify, remain unresolved, or return to an earlier possibility. These are available movements, not a required sequence. An unresolved distinction can remain open until it changes a consequence. Repetition and a new relationship are different observations.

An intuition can suggest a construction without proving its interpretation. Metaphor, assumption, hypothesis, prediction, observed consequence, and explanation are distinct. Agreement can arise from shared information rather than independent support. Apparent success can have rival explanations.

An error can expose a local assumption, representation, or operation without invalidating everything connected to it. Revision can preserve what still holds while changing what failed. Failure of an argument does not by itself settle its conclusion.

Persistence can reside in current conditions, accumulated history, or changed surroundings. Similar outcomes do not locate their cause. Compression can preserve some distinctions and erase others. A claim has a scope; uncertainty can remain explicit. Writing about an action and the consequences of performing it are different things.
geology: Sedimentary rocks form when grains settle and become compacted or cemented. Rivers carry sand and silt toward lower ground, while wind moves fine material across exposed surfaces. The speed of flowing water affects which grains remain suspended and which collect on the bed. Coarse gravel often settles near a strong current, and fine clay can travel much farther before settling. Layers may retain ripples, impressions, or fragments of older material. Burial can reduce the spaces between grains as overlying sediment adds weight. Dissolved minerals can precipitate in those spaces and bind neighboring grains together. Different minerals respond differently to weathering at the surface. Quartz commonly survives transport that breaks down less resistant minerals. Limestone can contain shells or other remains from organisms that lived in shallow seas. Sandstone often preserves evidence of beaches, river channels, or dunes. Mudstone can form in quieter water where fine particles accumulate. Changes in color may reflect mineral composition or chemical conditions during burial. Rock exposed at the surface can crack as temperatures change or water freezes within small openings. Roots can widen cracks, and flowing water can carry loose fragments away. Mountain building can lift buried layers and expose them to erosion again. Geological maps describe the distribution of rock units at the surface. A fresh broken surface can look different from an exterior surface that has weathered for a long time. Field descriptions often include grain size, mineral content, color, and the character of contacts between layers. Fossils can provide evidence about past environments and relative ages. Coastal cliffs sometimes expose broad sequences that are hidden beneath soil farther inland. Volcanic ash can settle between sedimentary beds, leaving a contrasting layer. Over long intervals, deposition, burial, uplift, and erosion can repeatedly change a landscape. Groundwater passes through connected spaces in permeable rocks and may dissolve minerals along its route. Springs occur where that water reaches the ground surface. The shape of a valley can reflect both the materials beneath it and the processes that have worn them away.
textiles: Woven cloth consists of crossing sets of yarn. Warp yarns extend along the length of the fabric, while weft yarns pass across its width. A loom keeps the warp under tension and provides a way to pass the weft through alternating openings. The arrangement of crossings produces different surface textures. Plain weave alternates over and under neighboring warp yarns. Twill arrangements produce diagonal lines, while satin arrangements spread the crossings to create a smoother visible surface. Fiber choice affects softness, strength, moisture absorption, and how a fabric hangs. Cotton fibers grow around seeds and can be spun into yarn after cleaning and preparation. Wool fibers have a crimped structure that contributes to warmth and resilience. Linen fibers come from flax stems and can produce a firm cloth with a distinctive texture. Silk consists of long fibers drawn from cocoons and is known for its smooth appearance. Synthetic fibers are produced from manufactured polymers and can have different lengths and cross sections. Yarn may be twisted more tightly to increase firmness or left more loosely twisted for a softer surface. Dye can be applied to fibers, yarn, or completed cloth. Washing and finishing can change the dimensions and feel of a woven fabric. A selvedge is the finished edge formed along the sides during weaving. Cut edges may unravel unless they are secured by stitching or another finish. Knitted fabrics use interlocking loops instead of the crossing arrangement of woven cloth. The loops allow many knitted materials to stretch readily. Felt can be made by pressing and working suitable fibers together without spinning them into yarn. Fabric inspection can reveal broken threads, uneven tension, or irregular color. Storage conditions influence how well textiles retain their appearance over time. Strong sunlight can fade dyes and weaken some fibers. Moisture and restricted airflow can encourage damage during storage. Garments are often cut with attention to the direction of the yarns because that direction affects drape. The same cloth can feel different when folded, gathered, or stretched across a curved surface. Seams join pieces of fabric, and their construction affects strength, flexibility, and the appearance of the finished item. Pressing can flatten seams and help set the intended shape. Care labels describe suitable washing, drying, and pressing conditions for the materials used.
